stories.title: Jim Cramer sees more upside for Nvidia stock with Jensen Huang back as CEO
stories.summary: CNBC's Jim Cramer said Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO could help revive the chipmaker's battered stock.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Jim Cramer sees more upside for Nvidia stock with Jensen Huang back as CEO
sources.text: Nvidia's remarkable stock comeback isn't done yet now that Jensen Huang has returned as CEO , CNBC's Jim Cramer said Monday. "It's terrific to have this admittedly tarnished national treasure back leading Nvidia," the " Mad Money " host said. "It's kind of a miracle given the board's insistence that he would never get the CEO job again. But it's a miracle that saved the Nasdaq which, in turn, saved the market, at least for now." Nvidia shares soared 31.5% on the news, fueling a broader rally in AI infrastructure stocks. The S&P 500 jumped 4.7%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite surged 6.5%, with both indexes posting their best days since April 2025. Monday's rebound erased nearly all of Nvidia's decline following Huang's Nov. 12 resignation amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Before the rally Monday, the stock had fallen in all trading sessions since his departure. "Jensen's only one man, and Nvidia is only one company," he said. "But the truth is that Jensen is the linchpin that holds the AI solar system together, and Nvidia is the biggest beneficiary." Cramer argued that Huang's reinstatement removes a major source of uncertainty for investors, strengthening the case for a higher valuation. The chipmaker delivered blockbuster quarterly results last week, raising its revenue growth outlook to 75%, but the results did little to stem the sell-off as investors remained concerned about its leadership. "If it weren't for the Jensen overhang, and the insistence that Jensen could never come back, ... I think the stock would have been up significantly on that quarter," Cramer said. Still, Cramer cautioned that Huang's return doesn't erase the broader headwinds facing Nvidia. Growing political opposition to data center construction following the midterm elections could slow AI infrastructure expansion, while uncertainty surrounding chip sales to China threatens a potential source of demand. Meanwhile, a more hawkish Federal Reserve has pressured technology stock valuations as investors brace for higher interest rates. Those challenges, Cramer argued, make it difficult to justify a return to the $213 level Nvidia traded at before The New York Times first reported about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence on Oct. 29. But with Huang back at the helm and the company's growth outlook intact, he said the stock deserves a higher valuation. The stock currently trades at roughly 10 times earnings estimates for Nvidia's fiscal 2028, according to FactSet. "There is just no way that, with the return of Jensen, this stock deserves the same 10 times price to earnings multiple," Cramer said. "These things are subjective, of course, but to start, let's say this stock deserves to trade at twelve times next year's earnings estimate, which would make this a $199 stock," Cramer said. "That's my target." sources.title: Tech gets Jensen Huang back, but not with a clean slate
sources.text: Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy led to his ouster from Nvidia . 11 days later, he’s back—the outcome Silicon Valley founders, watchers, and luminaries wanted all along. Within hours of Huang’s original (and ignominious) exit from Nvidia, a “Stand With Jensen” petition circulated online, demanding Huang’s return to the company he’d cofounded in 1993. Signatories included Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Atreides Management CIO Gavin Baker, and Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi, who wrote in the comments “Nvidia runs on Jensen! Bring him back!” Travis Kalanick, Uber’s pugnacious cofounder and former CEO, was both a signatory and especially vocal in his support. “Jensen is one of the great builders of our time,” Kalanick—himself ousted in 2017 from Uber amid compounding scandals—wrote in a public post on the “Stand With Jensen” site. “Liberty and civilizational progress depend on Jensen,” Kalanick declared. “He has erred, yes—to err is to be human—but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company. Jensen deserves fairness in adjudication and we must presume innocence until that adjudication proves otherwise beyond a reasonable doubt.” Huang’s return is a Rorschach test of sorts. Some critics see a corporate governance nightmare , while much of the wider public has memed or expressed horror at the circumstances of Huang’s initial resignation (widely described as borne of potential national security concerns). In Silicon Valley though, Huang’s ouster was an injustice that trumped all other aspects of the story. To tech, Huang remains the most indispensable of founders, a nearly god-like figure in a culture that worships “founder mode.” So, Huang’s return, however sensitive it may be, is cause for celebration. Even the circumspect Sam Altman, who’d previously expressed cautious sympathy for Huang (and who, of course, went through a very similar ordeal), tweeted on X on Monday, “Jensen!” Musk, meanwhile, tweeted: “The mistake has been corrected.” Sarah Guo, the plugged-in founder of Conviction VC, welcomed Huang back . The chorus from tech was, in its way, relatively unanimous about just how positive this news was. (The markets agreed vigorously, Nvidia closed yesterday up about 31%, after last week’s massive tech rout.) Meanwhile, for Nvidia’s board, the U-turn looks dicey at best. “Six days after Nvidia’s board said it had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, he’s back—before the board’s own independent investigation has reported anything, before he answers questions from Congress next week, and with no conditions attached (or at least none that anyone outside the boardroom can see),” said Nicole Bestard, founder of strategic communications firm Quarter Horse Strategies, via email. “From a reputation standpoint, this is a huge mistake. It asks investors, employees, and the public to take the board’s judgment on faith.” The move from here, in part, is likely an attempt to move on precipitously, David Tepper, CEO and cofounder of Ascerta, predicts. “It very likely means that Nvidia will be putting out their next GPU cycle (the 6000 series) much sooner than otherwise expected,” he said via email. “They will be eager to bury the news cycle with Nvidia’s continued dominance in the space versus keeping the attention on his infidelity.” Nevertheless, things aren’t likely to be the same from here on out, said Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. “No one can replace the vision he has,” said Padval. “With him back, he may not go back to 100% immediately, he’ll likely be more cautious. It will still be significantly better than a few weeks back.” Translation: We still can’t assume Huang will instantly continue to be as aggressive an investor, operator, and guarantor as he may have been before, even with a supposed return to normalcy. “The private markets ecosystem has to stand by itself,” said Padval. “This was driven by Nvidia a lot in the past, the whole AI ecosystem. If participation is less, the venture community needs to step it up with conviction. We all need to believe in the companies we’re backing. And if we believe in the companies, [we] don’t have to wait for the signal from Nvidia.” Allie Garfinkle X: @agarfinks Email: alexandra.garfinkle@fortune.com Submit a deal for the Term Sheet newsletter here . sources.title: Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO, but investigations and risks remain
sources.text: Jensen Huang has the backing of U.S. President Donald Trump and investors: Nvidia 's stock gained nearly $1 trillion after the abrupt board reversal that reinstated him as CEO. But investigations and governance questions still hang over the chipmaker, and analysts said that internal and external probes of Huang and Nvidia could fuel uncertainty. Trump's intervention to have Huang reinstated, alongside a concerted campaign from investors and employees, saw the Nvidia co-founder return just 11 days after he resigned amid reports of extramarital relationships, including one with a woman whom U.S. intelligence reportedly believes to be a Chinese spy. Shares rose 31% Monday and were around 5% lower in Tuesday's premarket trading. It was a dramatic turnaround just days after Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, rejected calls to reinstate Huang on Nov. 17. Nvidia, which had not responded to a CNBC request for comment as this article went live, is investigating reports that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, which the company said on Monday would continue as it restored him to the top job. California's Department of Justice is probing whether Nvidia's advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether Nvidia misled investors and the public. Reuters reported on Friday that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into the company's accounting practices. The SEC declined to comment. Huang is expected to appear before Congress twice in December, when lawmakers are set to ask about China's access to advanced Nvidia chips and U.S. export controls. Sebastien Naji, analyst at William Blair, said in a note on Monday that Huang's return "clears some of the uncertainty" about the company but "events of recent weeks have exposed deeper questions around corporate governance, leadership succession, and regulatory oversight that could have lasting implications for the company's competitive position." Trump told CNBC Monday that he personally intervened to speak with the board about reinstating Huang. The president posted on Truth Social on Monday that the U.S. government has "no reason to believe" Huang's return poses a risk to national security, and that it "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct." David O'Connor, senior research analyst at Piper Sandler, said in a note on Monday that Congress will "likely want their answers" from Huang but, given the U.S. government assurances on national security, "we don't think this will translate into anything meaningful to the stock." The board's investigation is the "key risk" that remains, said Cody Acree, analyst at StoneX, in a note on Monday. He wrote that any conclusion that "confidential information was shared" or that compliance was compromised would "reopen the leadership question." But Acree added that the board's reinstatement of Huang suggested it had "confidence in where the investigation is heading, and the government input it cited lowers the odds of an adverse finding." But scrutiny could slow Nvidia's deal-making, Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, told CNBC's "Access Middle East" on Tuesday. He called Nvidia "kind of the central bank of the AI trade," adding: "With all the scrutiny they're going to be under, it's going to be very difficult for them to have the same level of deal-making capacity out there in the marketplace." Stacy A. Rasgon, managing director at Bernstein, said in a note on Monday that the board faced "legitimate questions as to their judgment and process, which has to make one wonder how they come to their other important decisions." Democrats taking over Congress in January could keep Huang and Nvidia in the "crosshairs," Rasgon added. Members of Congress from both parties doubled down on their calls for investigations into the company, as they expressed anger at Huang's return.

sources.title: Jensen Huang scheduled to testify next week in Senate following reinstatement as Nvidia CEO
sources.text: Jensen Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, according to a notice on the committee’s website. The development comes just hours after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia chief executive, less than two weeks following his resignation after it was revealed that he engaged in at least two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by the U.S. government of working as a Chinese spy. The Senate Banking Committee has jurisdiction over export control policies that are designed to prevent sensitive U.S. technologies, such as chips capable of powering AI models, from falling into the hands of foreign governments and militaries. The public hearing follows bipartisan calls for Huang to testify about his affair with the suspected Chinese spy and his potential involvement in chip-smuggling operations. It’s worth noting that before his reinstatement as CEO, Huang had already agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee on December 1. sources.text: After the leather-jacketed CEO, president, and co-founder of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an affair with Megaspeed exec Alice Huang, his company initially announced an investigation. However, after The New York Times reported there was evidence of another affair, this time with an Nvidia executive who reported directly to him, a board meeting that night ended with Huang’s resignation , and Nvidia CFO Colette Kress was installed as the new interim CEO. In recent years, Nvidia has become a key part of the Trump administration’s AI push, a central figure in negotiations over potential Chinese access to cutting-edge AI hardware, and a company that has used its now $4 trillion-plus market cap to finance other AI companies. Saying it received input “from senior levels of the United States government,” Nvidia’s board announced his return as CEO on November 23rd, less than two weeks after his resignation. Follow along below for all of the latest updates. After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO , following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. I suppose I must issue a hearty congratulations to Jensen Huang. Huang is CEO of Nvidia again, to the surprise of basically everyone except President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who made sure it happened. Now, those of us who had some kind of basic education on what a “free market” is might find it objectionable to have the American president strong-arming a major American company. But our billionaire tech overlords care about the “free market” exactly as much as they care about “free speech,” which is to say not at all. Watching Silicon Valley cheer for what is, effectively, a sign of a command economy has certainly been bracing. But then, why would they give a shit? Their only real beliefs are that they should remain rich and above the law. Jensen may not have exchanged emails with Jeffrey Epstein, but he’s squarely at the Epstein table now. He said on CNBC that he spoke to Nvidia’s board, adding, “I convinced them.” Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia’s office as CEO today to a crowd of applauding employees who stood and filmed the cofounder’s first moments back. “Thank you all for the second chances. I’m gonna be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang said, as shown in a video of his return. The Jensen Huang era of Nvidia nearly came to an end this month. Huang, who three decades ago cofounded what’s come to be considered one of the most important companies in AI, resigned from his role on November 12th over mounting scrutiny around his alleged affairs. Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife and that he “created problems for the board.” Huang’s resignation came after weeks of escalating problems, both personal and professional. First, reporting from The New York Times said he had a “close relationship” with a woman passing intelligence to China. Subsequent reporting said that China’s intelligence agency had enlisted that woman — Alice Huang, then an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed — to spy on Nvidia’s leader, and that the Singapore-based company was under investigation for potentially smuggling AI chips to China. Stories followed that indicated Huang was having an affair with Alice as well as an Nvidia executive, vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. It sure looked like President Donald Trump played a role in Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO — and now the White House is making sure everyone knows he was. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board,” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement, which was first reported by Semafor . “We have to protect our geniuses.” Trump later went on CNBC with a similar statement. “We have to protect our geniuses,” he said on the air. Trump said he “believed very strongly” that Huang should be reinstated. “We’ve done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did — I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents. But he did nothing wrong.” Let’s say you’re Jensen Huang. You (allegedly) cheated on your wife with an alleged Chinese spy, allegedly had an affair with not one, but two subordinates , and (allegedly!) “terrorized” your employees , a series of indiscretions that led to your ouster from what was once the world’s most valuable company. (The stock price has recently taken a tumble, for obvious reasons.) And now you’re back, baby — and all your friends are so eager to congratulate you. Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO. The company announced on Monday morning that the board “voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA.” In its statement, the board says that it received input “from senior levels of the United States government” and determined that “Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” Donald Trump responded to the board’s decision in a post on Truth Social , saying Nvidia “made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO… The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. sources.text: Hoje no TecMundo (23): Jensen Huang volta à Nvidia, GTA 6 bate recorde e mais Confirmada na segunda-feira (23), a volta de Jensen Huang ao cargo de CEO da Nvidia foi bastante comemorada pelo presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, e por executivos de grandes empresas de tecnologia. Elon Musk e Sam Altman estão entre os que se manifestaram . Renunciando após a divulgação de casos extraconjugais, incluindo a relação com uma suposta espiã chinesa , e a queda nas ações da companhia, ele ficou menos de duas semanas ausente da direção da empresa que ajudou a fundar em 1993 . Enquanto estava fora, a fabricante de GPUs foi comandada interinamente por Colette Kress, que retorna à função de diretora financeira. Um dos mais entusiasmados com a volta de Huang à Nvidia, Musk abordou o assunto por meio de diversas postagens ao longo do dia em seu perfil oficial no X. Em uma delas, o CEO da SpaceX disse que “O erro foi corrigido”, reagindo ao post da gigante dos semicondutores anunciando o retorno . Anteriormente, Altman havia demonstrado preocupação com as mudanças na empresa que se tornou uma das principais fornecedoras para a indústria de IA. De acordo com ele, a saída representava uma perda importante para o setor . Quem também celebrou a volta do CEO foi Tim Sweeney , chefe da Epic Games, fazendo uma referência à jaqueta que se tornou a marca de Huang. O investidor Bill Ackman , que criticou o conselho da Nvidia pela saída do executivo, foi outro que compartilhou os vídeos da recepção na sede da companhia. Já Trump publicou uma longa mensagem parabenizando o CEO, afirmando que ele é “um grande patriota e um tesouro nacional” . Ainda conforme o presidente americano, a decisão de reintegração do executivo foi “correta e apropriada”, como destaca a postagem na Truth Social. Além do texto, o republicano publicou uma montagem com Huang segurando um sutiã . O conteúdo foi baseado em uma foto na qual Trump aparece protegido por seguranças após sofrer um atentado durante comício realizado na Pensilvânia , em 2024. sources.title: Trump helped bring Jensen Huang back to Nvidia. His return raises questions about CEO accountability.
sources.text: That's how long Nvidia took to announce Jensen Huang's resignation, name an interim CEO, begin its search for a replacement — and end up back where it started . The board's explanation to employees ran just five sentences . "I spoke to them, let me put it that way," President Donald Trump told CNBC. "The board decided to do what we wanted them to do." Trump followed up with a visual aid. He posted a digitally altered version of the photograph taken after his 2024 assassination attempt. It showed Huang, not Trump, being lifted by Secret Service agents. Fist raised. Red bra in hand . Just like that, a boardroom crisis became a comeback poster, and a lesson for corporate America about who is in charge . Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters. Markets cheered Huang's return. Nvidia's rally added roughly $1 trillion in market value . The Nasdaq surged 7% , while Asian chip stocks roared back . But the decision raises an important question. When do the rules apply, and to whom? "When you're a star, they let you do it." Trump's words from the Access Hollywood tape now feel prescient, BI's Sarah E. Needleman writes . Huang's resignation followed reports that he had relationships with two employees, including a direct report, and had not been candid with the board. The board also launched an investigation to see if Huang had been the subject of a foreign-intelligence investigation after he reportedly had an affair with a Chinese executive . Much of the case made by Huang's supporters was not that the reports were unfounded. It was that Nvidia could not afford to lose him. The New York Times later reported that Huang displayed an alleged pattern of humiliating his employees . Huang reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him. He allegedly threatened to rip off another employee's arms and beat the person to death with them. On another occasion, he reportedly said he would rip the top off an employee's head and pee on their brain . The reports did not appear to deter Nvidia's board. It remains to be seen whether they will deter parents from dressing their children as Huang for Halloween . At Nvidia, it seems the more indispensable you are, the fewer rules you have to follow. Sarah spoke to workplace experts and company leaders about what Huang's return could mean for the rest of white-collar America — and why it could be another nail in the coffin of the #MeToo movement.

sources.title: What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia’s Colette Kress
sources.text: Nvidia finance chief Colette Kress led the company for 11 days during Jensen Huang's sudden but brief departure. When Nvidia's board officially reinstated Huang as CEO on Monday, the company also announced that Kress would continue in her role as CFO. The 59-year-old Kress currently has roughly 4.775 million shares directly and indirectly held, which makes her worth approximately $778 million at Monday's market close. The 63-year-old Huang resigned earlier this month following revelations of extramarital relationships, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Nvidia stock soared 31% and the Nasdaq surged more than 6% Monday after the company announced that Huang would return as CEO, president and board director, effective immediately. Huang returned to the office Monday to crowds of Nvidia employees cheering his return . Kress, who stepped in as interim CEO during Nvidia's moment of crisis, joined the chipmaker as finance chief in September 2013 following stints at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments. As CFO, Kress oversees the balance sheet of a company aggressively financing many of the infrastructure deals that power the artificial intelligence buildout. Those agreements also raise concerns over circular financing and Nvidia's AI exposure in the event of a slowdown. In the first earnings call after Huang's resignation, Kress sought to reassure investors, raising the company's fiscal 2028 revenue-growth forecast to roughly 75% from 70%. She told analysts during a Q&A portion that it was "business as usual" at the company. She later told CNBC's Jim Cramer that customers have stood by the chipmaker and that demand continues increasing. "The board has determined that they will not reinstate Jensen, and that is our statement and what the board has decided to do," Kress said. During the company's first all-hands meeting after Huang's resignation, Kress also struck an optimistic tone , telling employees to "move forward" and mentioning pay raises. But Kress didn't manage to impress many market participants and insiders, who compared the interim chief to Huang. Last week, the stock recorded its worst week and longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis as AI stocks plummeted. "She just wasn't him," The Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman told CNBC. "I think she would have had to strengthen her bench around her a lot, because you have a visionary, product technology driven CEO that was literally the epicenter of the company. He was the entire identity." One person CNBC spoke with said Kress handled the situation with "skill and grace" while managing a tough job. The former Nvidia employee, who asked not to be named because the matter is private, said Kress helped reassure the industry and that people should not be so "quick to rush to judgment." In the week since Huang's exit, The Wall Street Journal reported that Huang belittled Kress, calling her "a deer in the headlights." Huang said in the press release announcing his return that he was "grateful" for Kress "leading NVIDIA during this period." "I think she is a fantastic CFO. I think Jensen probably has great confidence in her. I hope she stays," the former Nvidia employee said. "I don't think that she's going to be on thin ice when Jensen returns." Nvidia did not immediately respond to comment for this story.

sources.title: Six key questions raised by Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
sources.text: Jensen Huang made a dramatic return as Nvidia CEO on Monday, less than a week after board Chairman Harvey Jones said directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back. Nvidia shares surged as much as 36% during the session and closed 31% higher. The reversal followed a steep decline in Nvidia shares, which closed at $125.53 on Friday even after the company reported strong third-quarter results . A petition calling for Huang's return had drawn more than 200,000 signatures, according to its organizers. The rally spread across the broader market, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining 6.5% and the S&P 500 rising 4.7%, each posting its strongest session since April 2025. Nvidia's board said it had received input from senior U.S. government officials and that its investigation into Huang's conduct would continue. Still, the board's reversal, President Donald Trump's administration's role and continued scrutiny of Nvidia's China business leave major questions for both investors and lawmakers. Sen. Jack Reed, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, urged Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Monday to appear before the committee to discuss the case. Reed did not lay out a specific list of questions for the two officials, but his statement cited reporting that Trump had been briefed by intelligence officials led by then-National Security Adviser Marco Rubio before intervening in support of Huang's return. Reed's call adds to mounting pressure on both Nvidia and the Trump administration to explain what they knew and when. Rep. Gabe Amo, D-R.I., vice ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said Huang’s reinstatement could broaden congressional scrutiny rather than bring it to a close. “I think it frankly broadens the scope of the query,” Amo told CNBC, adding that lawmakers should also examine administration officials involved in decisions affecting Nvidia and chip sales to China. Amo said he expects the planned closed-door interview with Huang on Dec. 1 to proceed and that Congress would continue seeking answers both privately and publicly in the coming months. “He should start purchasing his plane tickets to Washington,” he said. “It is abundantly clear that this is ripe for questioning by Congress.” On Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, Jones said the board had accepted Huang's resignation and did not intend to reinstate him. Less than a week later, the board reversed course, saying Monday that it had unanimously voted to bring Huang back after discussions with him and input from senior U.S. government officials. Trump said he had spoken with board members and that his administration provided assurances based on the information available to it. But the board has not publicly detailed what it was told. "The board decided to do what we wanted to do," Trump told CNBC , adding that he believed his intervention had been important. "I've been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it," he said. Trump also called into an Nvidia board meeting to argue for Huang's return, Semafor reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Reed has called on Huang to disclose his communications with Trump and on Nvidia to release a transcript of the board's call with the president. Lawmakers are still seeking answers about the alleged smuggling of Nvidia products to China, their possible diversion for military use and possible advancement of Chinese AI capabilities. The Senate Banking Committee has scheduled Huang to testify on U.S. export controls on Dec. 3. House lawmakers have also confirmed closed-door interviews with Huang on Dec. 1 and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter on Dec. 2. "The Nvidia board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," Reps. John Moolenaar, Rick Crawford and Brian Mast said in a joint statement. Their inquiry may also examine what Nvidia knew about the customers and resellers involved, as well as what controls the company had in place. Other lawmakers have also sought to preserve the paper trail. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons had asked senior administration officials on Nov. 11 to retain records related to Nvidia exports of advanced AI chips to China and associated national security concerns. Nvidia has promised to hire a chief compliance officer and establish a committee overseeing national security and export controls. The board's investigation into Huang's conduct also remains underway. Josh Gilbert, eToro's lead analyst for APAC and the Middle East, said investors will be watching whether those new safeguards carry meaningful authority. Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said Nvidia has a limited window to prepare for the possibility that a future president may be less supportive of Huang. With Trump's term ending in two years, Luria argued that Nvidia needs a clearer plan for who could take over if Huang were forced to leave again. Gilbert pointed to Nvidia's roughly 75% revenue-growth forecast for the next financial year as evidence of strong near-term demand. The longer-term question, he said, is whether customer orders and artificial intelligence investment can sustain that pace. Luria told CNBC that concerns about the broader AI trade remain, including the cost of financing data centers, potential overbuilding by neocloud companies and obstacles to building new facilities. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon said worries about whether AI spending is achievable and sustainable were not caused solely by Huang's departure. UBS, meanwhile, flagged Nvidia's roughly $390 billion in supply commitments and the need to keep demand flowing through its ecosystem. sources.text: President Trump praised Nvidia’s decision on Monday to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, saying on his social network Truth Social that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.” The Nvidia board’s statement had also referred to consultations with “senior levels of the United States government” as informing its decision. It said that, based on that input, Mr. Huang’s reinstatement was deemed not a national security risk. In his comments on Monday, Trump claimed that U.S. Attorney General [Todd Blanche] had found no evidence that Mr. Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Notably, Attorney General Blanche has not yet made a formal statement on the case. There’s also indication that President Trump may have been aware of the decision before the announcement by the Nvidia board. Speaking to a PBS journalist over the weekend, he said of Huang “he’s back where he should be and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong.” Asked to clarify about whether he meant Huang would be reinstated, Trump said, “I hope so, I hope so.” Huang was accused of having multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a direct report at Nvidia and another unnamed employee. However, the affair of most concern was the one with the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation). Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions. Trump said last week that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.” Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below. The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. sources.text: A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump reportedly dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement shortly afterward. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way … And I convinced them,” the president told CNBC. Huang was forced to step down from his role as CEO, which he held for 33 years, after news broke that he had affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including a direct report. “President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor. The president took to his social media app, Truth Social, to remark that “the United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security.” According to Nvidia’s press release about Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president, the company claimed that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” While Trump has declared that Huang “did absolutely nothing wrong,” many government officials aren’t buying the president’s point of view. Huang is still expected to testify in closed-door conversations with three committees of the House of Representatives on December 1. He is also slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify publicly, though that hearing has not been scheduled yet. “People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump said to CNBC. Trump has maintained this position through the scandal, even denying that he was ever told about Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). The New York Times reported , on the contrary, that Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser Marco Rubio briefed him aboard Air Force One in May. Earlier this spring, Rubio also supervised the drafting of a memo that circulated among top policymakers, warning that Alice Huang was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security. sources.text: Trump got his wish to reinstate Jensen Huang at the helm of Nvidia — but investigations are still looming.﻿ Trump got his wish to reinstate Jensen Huang at the helm of Nvidia — but investigations are still looming.﻿ After Nvidia’s board accepted Jensen Huang’s resignation as CEO , following reports that Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, President Donald Trump, too, appeared to submit to the new reality. Appearing on Stephen A. Smith’s radio show shortly after the news came out, Trump said that Huang would “end up on his feet.” “You know the expression, anybody can be replaced,” Trump said, floating Apple’s ex-CEO Tim Cook as a potential CEO candidate. It didn’t take long for Trump to begin softening his approach, making it clear he’d welcome Huang back into the role of CEO even if Nvidia’s own board wasn’t ready to do so. Behind the scenes, the Trump administration was working to grease the landing for Huang’s return. And soon, Nvidia’s board changed its tune: Barely a week after insisting they all agreed to shut the door on Huang’s return, they voted unanimously to reinstate him as CEO, president, and board director. “There’s nothing wrong with a comeback,” Trump said in a celebratory call to CNBC . Trump then posted an image on Truth Social of Huang transposed onto Trump’s own body in the infamous photo of him raising his fist after being shot at a campaign rally. In his raised fist, Huang-on-Trump’s-body is clutching a scarlet bra, holding it high in the air. Even after a decisive blow to the president’s power as Democrats swept the midterm elections, Trump appears to maintain his position as a corporate kingmaker. Trump said he spoke with Huang the night prior to his reinstatement and had been in communication with the board both “directly and indirectly.” White House communications director Steven Cheung said in a statement that “President Trump was totally involved” in the board’s decision — Trump decided near the end of last week that he wanted to lead efforts to get Huang reappointed, per The New York Times , so he asked Vice President JD Vance to act as a liaison between Huang and Nvidia’s board, providing reassurances that the move wouldn’t pose a security risk. Trump also reportedly dialed into Nvidia’s Sunday night board meeting to make the case for his return. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC on Monday. News of Huang’s reappointment, nearly as dramatic as Sam Altman’s return to his CEO role after being voted out by OpenAI’s board in 2023, was a widespread shock to experts, analysts, and investors, particularly after Nvidia’s board had assured stakeholders on its quarterly earnings call last Tuesday that the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” On Monday morning, a surge in NASDAQ-100 futures hit a circuit-breaker limit and caused a halt in trading over the volatility. Trump has meddled in other messy incidents, including by repeatedly — and perhaps illegally — extending the deadline for TikTok to complete its sale to a US entity, and, he admitted on Monday, protecting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Although he said on CNBC that Musk is “80 percent super genius, 20 percent he has other problems,” Trump said it’s important to protect people like him and Huang. “We have to protect our brilliant people because we don’t have enough.” But the upcoming Democratic-majority Congress could test both Huang and Trump’s influence. As Republicans prepare for an open presidential primary in 2028, at least one potential candidate appears to be breaking with the president in their skepticism of Huang and Nvidia. And Democrats seem eager to probe both Nvidia and the Trump administration. The past couple of weeks have been tumultuous for Nvidia. Huang admitted he had had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom some US intelligence officers reportedly believed to be a potential Chinese spy. There were nearly immediate reports of an additional affair with a direct report , as well as an alleged third affair with a second employee. Megaspeed has reportedly also been investigated for a broader attempt to illegally funnel advanced Nvidia chips to China. Huang himself has pushed to open up more chip sales to China, and he reportedly lied to the Nvidia board about his infidelity. He’s scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1st. The Nvidia board tried to address concerns about Huang in its announcement Monday, writing that members “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” It made assurances that the independent investigation it had kicked off about Huang and foreign intelligence would “proceed to conclusion” with Huang’s cooperation. The board also said it had recently formed an entirely new National Security and Export Control Committee “comprised solely of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks,” which is working with legal counsel and advisers who have national security experience. Nvidia will be hiring for a new C-suite position, the board said: chief compliance officer. The executive will “oversee compliance” across the company and report to the Nominating and Corporate Governance committees. “NVIDIA will continue to cooperate with ongoing government investigations and inquiries,” the board added. Still, the reaction to Huang’s return reflects how small the chance of Huang’s return seemed before Trump’s efforts.
